cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-100-chris.summary: The cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, holding a book, staff and rod, stands on a hill with three angels and turns toward the psalmist, who points to the faithful seated around an empty throne: 'mine eyes shall be upon the faithful of the land'. Behind the psalmist a man holds an open book for him to sing from — 'I will sing of mercy and judgment'. It is the lower drawing on folio 57v.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-100-chris.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server. This folio carries two drawings; the crop shows the one for this text.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-147-chris.summary: The cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, carrying a cross-staff and attended by angels with bannered wands, leans out of heaven to bless the psalmist and the children of Jerusalem standing on the walled hill of Sion: 'he hath blessed thy children within thee'. Angels bring down his word and his wind, snow and hoar frost fall on the hills, and warriors lay down their shields and carry palms in token of peace.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-147-chris.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-nunc-dimittis-p.summary: For the Song of Simeon the artist shows the Virgin holding out the Christ child across an altar to the aged Simeon, who receives him, with Anna behind Simeon and Joseph bringing doves; rays from the altar fall on a group of people, 'a light to lighten the Gentiles'. It is the upper drawing of folio 89v and an early image of the Presentation in the Temple.

cur:manuscripts2-stuttgart-psalter-psalm.summary: On a green ground a youthful, haloed Christ sits on a hillock and gestures as he speaks to a bearded man holding a book, while two more figures approach from the right. The miniature illustrates the verse written just above it, 'Audi populus meus et loquar' — 'Hear, O my people, and I will speak ... I am God, even thy God'.
facts: The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
cur:manuscripts2-stuttgart-psalter-psalm.notes: The haloed speaker is identified as Christ following the psalter's consistent practice of showing the Lord of the psalms as the youthful Christ; the halo shows no cross. The image is the full page; the miniature occupies only part of it.

wga:zearly/1/2mural/3priscil/2velati7.summary: At the centre of the ceiling of the Cubiculum of the Velata, framed by a red circle, a youthful shepherd in a short tunic carries a sheep on his shoulders and stretches out his hand, while a sheep or goat stands on each side and doves perch in the trees above. The gentle, symmetrical composition presides over the chamber's scenes of a Christian woman's life and prayer, placing her under the care of Christ the Good Shepherd.
facts: The chamber takes its name (Velata or Velatio, 'the veiled woman') from the praying, veiled woman painted on its end wall.
The Catacomb of Priscilla on the Via Salaria was used for Christian burials from the late 2nd to the 4th century and was known in antiquity as the 'Queen of the Catacombs'.
wga:zearly/1/2mural/3priscil/2velati7.notes: WGA dates this to 'around 200'; Commons/Wikidata (for the same ceiling) give the second half of the 3rd century (Wikidata 275), which is the more usual dating for the Velata cubiculum. Same ceiling as Q110184746 in this batch, which is marked as a duplicate of this entry.
